name: Omea Analytics
author: Cultmetrics

sections.description:
Omea Analytics measures your WordPress site without sending anything to third parties – the data stays in your own database. Without consent it is cookieless (the same approach as Matomo’s cookieless mode); with a visitor’s Statistics consent it also recognises returning visitors and credits conversions to the campaign that first brought them.

It is built to be the fastest analytics plugin for WordPress: a 1.8 KB tracker (gzip) that sends two requests per page, a collector that stores hits without loading WordPress, and reports read from daily rollups – a 30-day dashboard on a busy site loads in milliseconds, and history stays exact after visit-level data is deleted.

What you get

  • Visits, visitors, pageviews, bounce and engagement rate, time on page and scroll depth, in your site’s time zone.
  • Channels aligned with GA4 – including AI Assistants (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot, Claude) – plus source, medium, campaign, term and content, referring domains and ad click IDs (Google, Microsoft, Meta, TikTok, LinkedIn, X).
  • Entry and exit pages, page detail with where visitors came from and went next.
  • Goals and conversions from page visits, clicks, forms and custom events (omea.trackEvent(), data-omea-event), with conversion rate and revenue per goal and channel. WooCommerce purchases, checkouts and add-to-carts are recorded on the server – a purchase counts even when the buyer never returns to the thank-you page.
  • Countries, regions and cities from a local database on your server; browsers, operating systems (including Windows 11) and screen sizes.
  • New vs returning visitors and visit frequency for visitors who gave Statistics consent.
  • Bot traffic filtered before anything is stored – crawlers, scripts, automated browsers and vulnerability scanners – with a counter of what was filtered.
  • Automatic outbound-link, download, email/phone-click and site-search tracking, pages not found (404), and Content reports by author, category and post type.
  • AI crawlers: how often GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and others fetch your pages – next to the visits AI assistants send you.
  • Core Web Vitals from real visitors (sampled): LCP, INP, CLS and TTFB per page.
  • Import your history from Koko Analytics, WP Statistics, Burst Statistics, Independent Analytics, Statify, Slimstat, Jetpack Stats, Plausible or Google Analytics 4.
  • CSV export of every report, chart notes, saved segments, a weekly email report, a dashboard widget, a Views column, a Popular posts block, WP-CLI, a read-only Reporting API (Google Sheets, Looker Studio) and MCP abilities for AI assistants.
  • View-only access for the roles you choose; multisite network overview.
  • A “Get set up” checklist that tells you when something needs attention: geolocation database, tracking, collector, visitor IP behind a CDN, consent setup, conversions, privacy policy.

Privacy

Without consent (default): cookieless. No cookies, no localStorage, nothing in the browser. A visit is recognised on your server by a one-way hash of the IP address (the /64 network for IPv6), browser, language and site under a random key that is replaced every day; the old key is deleted half an hour after midnight, so visits can’t be linked across days or traced back to an IP address. The IP address is never stored. Many data protection authorities, such as France’s CNIL, accept cookieless audience measurement like this without consent – check the guidance in your country. If you prefer, choose “Record nothing before consent” (enforced on the server too).

With Statistics consent: returning visitors. When a visitor explicitly accepts Statistics in Omea Consent or a plugin that uses the WordPress Consent API, the server sets a first-party HttpOnly cookie omea_vid holding a random ID (13 months by default; 1–25 months, or turn it off). Only a keyed hash of that ID is stored. Withdrawing consent removes the cookie.

What is stored: page path (no query string), referrer host and path, UTM parameters, the type of ad click ID (never its value), coarse device type, OS and browser family, screen-size bucket, ISO country code, region and city. No IP addresses, no coordinates. Server-side events (purchases, sign-ups) never store user, order or contact IDs.

Retention: visit-level hits are deleted after 30 days and visits after 395 days by default (both configurable); daily reports without visitor data are kept.

External services

Omea Analytics makes no external requests while it measures – visits are recognised on your server, and locations come from a local database file or your host’s/CDN’s headers.

  • DB-IP City Lite (default geolocation) – After activation, when you select DB-IP, and once a month when a new release is published, the plugin downloads the free DB-IP City Lite database from https://download.db-ip.com/free/ via WP-Cron. Only the download request is made: no visitor data and no site address is sent. Lookups then run locally. The file is stored in a private, randomly named folder in uploads. Choose “Proxy / CDN headers only” in Settings › Geolocation to avoid this. IP geolocation by DB-IP (https://db-ip.com), licensed under CC BY 4.0.

  • MaxMind GeoLite2 / GeoIP2 (optional) – Only when selected and your own MaxMind account ID and licence key are entered: the database is downloaded from https://download.maxmind.com/ and refreshed weekly. MaxMind’s licence requires using a release no older than 30 days, so a copy that cannot be updated for 30 days is removed. Terms: https://www.maxmind.com/en/geolite2/eula

  • Jetpack Stats import (optional) – Only when an administrator starts an import from Jetpack Stats on a site connected to WordPress.com: the plugin asks WordPress.com, through Jetpack’s own connection, for that site’s daily views, visitors, top posts, referrers and countries. Nothing else is sent. WordPress.com terms: https://wordpress.com/tos/ – privacy: https://automattic.com/privacy/

Files the plugin writes

  • omea-analytics-collect.php in the site root – a few lines that pass tracker hits to the plugin’s collector without loading WordPress (the same approach as other fast analytics plugins). It is removed when the plugin is deactivated. If the site root isn’t writable, or on multisite, hits go to the plugin’s REST endpoint instead. Define OMEA_ANALYTICS_NO_COLLECTOR to turn it off.
  • wp-content/omea-analytics/ – the collector’s settings and a short-lived buffer of hits (stored into the database every minute), in randomly named files that deny web access.
  • wp-content/uploads/omea-analytics/ – the geolocation database.
sections.installation:
1. Upload the plugin through the Plugins screen, or copy the plugin folder into wp-content/plugins/.
  2. Activate Omea Analytics. The geolocation database downloads in the background.
  3. Open Omea Analytics › Dashboard and follow the “Get set up” checklist.

The plugin ships with all compiled assets and required libraries; no build tools are needed to run it.
sections.faq:
Does this plugin set cookies?

Not without consent. With a visitor’s explicit Statistics consent (Omea Consent or a WP Consent API plugin), the server sets a first-party HttpOnly cookie omea_vid holding a random ID, to recognise returning visitors. You can turn this off in Settings › Privacy; then the plugin never sets cookies.

Does it store IP addresses or full user agents?

No. The IP address is used only on your server, for the location lookup and the daily visit hash, and is never stored. User agents are reduced to device type, OS and browser family.

Will the numbers match Google Analytics?

They will be close but not identical: Omea filters bots before storing anything, counts visitors without consent cookielessly (a returning visitor without consent counts again the next day), and isn’t blocked by most ad blockers because it runs on your own domain.

How are bots kept out?

Pageviews are counted by the browser tracker, so bots that don’t run JavaScript never appear. Crawlers, scripts, automated browsers and vulnerability scanners that do are filtered out before anything is stored. Settings › Tracking shows how many were filtered.

My site is behind Cloudflare or another proxy – are locations right?

Yes: Cloudflare is detected automatically, and other proxies’ X-Forwarded-For headers are read safely. If your host uses a different header, pick it in Settings › Advanced › Visitor IP header; the checklist warns when it looks wrong.

I use a caching or optimisation plugin – anything to do?

Exclude omea-tracker from “delay JavaScript” features. For WP Rocket, LiteSpeed Cache, Perfmatters and FlyingPress the plugin adds the exclusion automatically; the checklist tells you if something else blocks tracking.

Old data isn’t deleted on my site – why?

Cleanup and the minute-by-minute storing of hits run with WordPress’ scheduler (WP-Cron), which only runs when someone visits the site. On a quiet site, or if WP-Cron is disabled, set up a real cron job that calls wp-cron.php (for example every 5 minutes) – most hosts offer this in their control panel.

Can I disable tracking for admins?

Yes. Settings › Tracking includes an option to skip tracking for administrators.

Is it translated? Does it work with Polylang or WPML?

Every screen, the dashboard and the email report are translatable on translate.wordpress.org, and numbers and dates follow your language. On multilingual sites (Polylang, or WPML) the dashboard gets a Languages report, the Popular posts block lists posts in the page’s language (optionally ranking a post by the views of all its translations), and the email report is sent in each recipient’s language.
sections.changelog:
0.7.0

  • Rebuilt for correct numbers: one record per visit with its source decided once, no lost events or conversions, server-side revenue, site time zone, accurate sources (AI Assistants channel, ad click IDs, search engines in every country), Cloudflare/proxy-aware visitor IPs.
  • With Statistics consent: returning visitors, visit frequency and first-touch attribution (first-party HttpOnly cookie, only with consent). Without consent: cookieless as before.
  • Faster: 1.8 KB tracker with two requests per page, a collector that stores hits without loading WordPress, and lossless daily rollups (dashboard in milliseconds).
  • New reports: cities and regions, browsers, operating systems, screen sizes, campaigns, referring domains, entry and exit pages, goals with revenue, events, hour of day, new vs returning visitors.
  • “Get set up” checklist; the geolocation database downloads and updates automatically; WooCommerce purchases count even without the thank-you page.
  • Outbound links, downloads, site search, 404s, Content by author/category/post type, AI crawlers and Core Web Vitals.
  • Importers (Koko, WP Statistics, Burst, Independent Analytics, Statify, Slimstat, Jetpack, Plausible, GA4), CSV export, chart notes, saved segments, email reports, dashboard widget, Views column, Popular posts block, WP-CLI, Reporting API, MCP abilities and view-only roles.
  • Translatable everywhere; Polylang/WPML: Languages report, Popular posts in the page’s language, email report in each recipient’s language. Fixed: visits on a language’s own domain (Polylang/WPML) were dropped.

0.6.0

  • Cookieless by design: no cookies or browser storage. Visits are recognised by a daily-rotating salted hash (Matomo-style); the IP address is never stored.
  • Pageviews always come from the browser tracker – works with page caching, and bots that don’t run JavaScript are never counted.
  • Bot traffic excluded: crawlers, scripts, automated browsers and vulnerability scanners are filtered, with a 30-day counter and a one-click cleanup of bot visits already in your history.
  • New: choose what happens before Statistics consent – measure cookieless (default) or record nothing (now enforced on the server too, and the page is counted as soon as the visitor allows statistics).
  • Data minimisation: referrers without query strings, no coordinates, no user/order/contact ids in server-side events, geolocation debug never stores the IP or request headers.
  • Hardened event endpoint: own-site hits only, rate limit per visitor, smaller batches, no location data in responses, proxy headers trusted only from private/known proxies.
  • Retention now also clears visit links from daily totals and conversions; uninstall removes downloaded geolocation databases.
  • Faster: schema checks run once per version instead of on every request; bot counts use atomic updates in their own table.
  • Settings › General shows when old data was last cleaned up.

0.5.0

  • New: Conversions screen – count a visit to a thank-you page, a click, a form submission or an event as a conversion, with an optional value. Turn any logged event into a conversion in one click.
  • New: Server-side events moved to the Conversions screen; WooCommerce purchases, checkouts and add-to-carts are listed automatically when WooCommerce is active.
  • New: One JavaScript API for all Omea plugins – omea.trackEvent(‘name’) and data-omea-event=”name”.
  • New: Works together with Omea Consent Pro, which can send the same conversions to ad platforms with the visitor’s consent.
  • Redesigned admin screens.

0.4.0

  • Clarified privacy documentation for cookieless-capable and short-lived cookie-based operation.
  • Session attribution moved server-side; removed persistent client-side browser storage.
  • Admin dashboard assets now load only on Omea Analytics screens.
  • Chart.js and the geo chart library are served locally only (no CDN fallback).
  • Removed verbose debug logging from the frontend tracker and admin bundles.
  • Documented optional external geolocation services and refreshed privacy details.

0.2.1

  • Initial public release candidate with REST-driven dashboard, aggregation, and settings UI.
